answer:
An in-kind ETF can meet large redemptions by delivering stocks to an authorized participant instead of selling them for cash. Under RIC rules, qualifying in-kind redemptions generally don’t make the fund recognize gains on appreciated securities distributed; selecting low-basis lots can reduce embedded gains. A cash-dealing mutual fund more often sells holdings to meet redemptions, potentially realizing gains distributed and taxed that year.

This can defer or reduce fund-level realized gains, but doesn’t guarantee zero capital-gain distributions. It doesn’t eliminate taxable dividends, gains from sales or portfolio changes, or tax when investors sell ETF shares at a gain. Benefits depend on flows, turnover, gains, and in-kind redemption capacity. Investors may owe tax on distributions even if reinvested. Mutual funds may also avoid sales when they have cash or offsetting losses.
original_answer:
An in-kind ETF can meet large redemptions by delivering a basket of stocks to an authorized participant rather than selling stocks for cash. Under the RIC rules, a qualifying in-kind redemption generally does not make the fund recognize gain on appreciated securities distributed; the fund can select low-basis lots, reducing embedded gains. A cash-dealing mutual fund more often sells holdings to fund redemptions, realizing gains that may be distributed to shareholders and taxed in the year received.

This is a deferral/reduction of fund-level realized gains—not a guarantee of zero capital-gain distributions. It does not eliminate taxable dividends, gains the fund realizes in sales or portfolio changes, or tax when an investor sells ETF shares at a gain. Benefits vary with flows, turnover, gains, and the ETF’s ability to redeem in kind; investors can also owe tax on distributions even if they reinvest them. The mutual fund may likewise avoid sales when it has cash or offsetting losses.
